title: Institutional modelling: Adding social backbone to agent-based models
publisher: MethodsX (Elsevier), via PMC; author Amineh Ghorbani (TU Delft)

key_points.claim: Institutional modelling is a branch of ABMS that explicitly models institutions (social structure/rules) as the social backbone of simulated societies, combining bottom-up agent behaviour with top-down structure.
key_points.evidence_quote: While agent-based modelling is a bottom-up (individual-based) simulation approach, institutional modelling also incorporates top-down institutional structures

key_points.claim: Institutions are conceptualized with the Institutional Grammar (ABDICO): Attribute, Deontic, Aim, Object, Condition, Or else.
key_points.evidence_quote: Each statement consists of a maximum of 6 components.

key_points.claim: Three institution types are distinguished: rules (A-D-I-C-O, explicit sanction), norms (A-D-I-C), shared strategies (A-I-C, no deontic or sanction).
key_points.evidence_quote: Shared Strategies (A-I-C): an institutional statement with no sanction (similar to norms) and no deontic attached to it

key_points.claim: Institutions should be modelled as independent entities, not inside agents: they are common knowledge, context-specific, can be deliberated on/disobeyed/sanctioned, and can be interlinked.
key_points.evidence_quote: institutions, at least at the conceptualization phase should be modelled as independent entities, not as part of agent behaviour

key_points.claim: Institutional data are qualitative and hard to collect. Methods include interviews/ethnography for informal institutions and IG coding of legal documents (6-step guideline from Basurto et al.) for formal ones.
key_points.evidence_quote: data about institutions is not easy to collect to incorporate into a model given its qualitative nature

key_points.claim: Agent decisions can incorporate institutions' deontic, condition and sanction via standard decision frameworks (theory of planned behaviour, multi-criteria decision making). Conditions link physical environment and social context.
key_points.evidence_quote: This decision can be modelled with any decision making framework such as Theory of planned behaviour or Multi-criteria decision making.

key_points.claim: Institutions can be static (hard-coded) or dynamic (agents change or create institutions, so structures emerge). This enables studying evolution between shared strategies, norms and rules, and institutional change.
key_points.evidence_quote: By allowing agents to use a language to define institutions, these social structures are not pre-defined by the modeller but are emergent from the simulation.

key_points.claim: Recommended use cases for detailed institutional modelling are policy analysis, institutional dynamics (e.g., commons self-organization with agents voting on rules) and collective behaviour patterns.
key_points.evidence_quote: The agents collectively define institutions by voting: i.e., they suggest their own individual strategy as the preferred rule.

key_points.claim: Institutions can form networks that define relationships between actors. Hierarchies of institutions are possible because the 'or else' can itself be an institutional statement.
key_points.evidence_quote: In that case, the “or else” component can itself be another institutional statement.

reliability_notes: Full text, open access (CC BY), peer-reviewed methods paper. It is a single-author methodological overview centred on the author's own approach (IG/MAIA), not a broad survey. It has few empirical results and is self-citation heavy.
